0. Set-up¶

What: import the libraries and fix a few settings. Why: each library has one job, and a fixed random seed makes our results reproducible: anyone who runs this notebook gets the same numbers as our report. How: the imports are grouped by purpose.

Library Job in this project
pandas, numpy Tables and numbers
matplotlib All the charts
scikit-learn Preprocessing, the models, tuning and the metrics
joblib Saving the trained model to a file
In [1]:

What: read the California Housing CSV into a pandas table and look at it. Why: before any modelling we must know what we have: how big it is, what the columns mean, and whether anything is missing or odd. How: pd.read_csv loads the file. 2. Exploratory data analysis (EDA)¶

What: draw charts to understand each feature and how features relate to price. Why: EDA tells us what to fix (missing values, skew), what to create (new features) and which models are likely to work. It is much cheaper to learn this from a chart than from a failed model. How: every chart below is plain matplotlib: hist for distributions, scatter for relationships, imshow for the heatmap, bar for categories.

3. Feature engineering and preprocessing¶

3.1 New features (feature engineering)¶

What: create three ratio features. Why: raw totals mostly tell us how big a neighbourhood is. Price depends on what a typical home looks like, so we divide by the number of households. How: simple column arithmetic in pandas. Then we check the correlation to confirm the ratios are really more useful.

In [11]:
data = df.copy()
data["rooms_per_household"]      = data["total_rooms"] / data["households"]        # typical home size
data["bedrooms_per_room"]        = data["total_bedrooms"] / data["total_rooms"]    # high share = small, cheaper homes
data["population_per_household"] = data["population"] / data["households"]         # crowding

check = data[["total_rooms", "rooms_per_household", "bedrooms_per_room", "population_per_household",
              "median_house_value"]].corr()["median_house_value"].drop("median_house_value")
print("Correlation with price:")
print(check.round(3))

Correlation with price:
total_rooms                 0.134
rooms_per_household         0.152
bedrooms_per_room          -0.256
population_per_household   -0.024
Name: median_house_value, dtype: float64

rooms_per_household (+0.15) already beats raw total_rooms (+0.13), and bedrooms_per_room (−0.26) is clearly stronger: feature engineering paid off before we trained anything.

3.2 Train / test split¶

What: hide 20% of the neighbourhoods from the models. Why: a model must be judged on data it has never seen; otherwise we only measure memory, not learning. How: train_test_split with test_size=0.2 and a fixed seed. We stratify by price level (Low / Medium / High thirds) so both sets contain a similar mix of cheap and expensive areas.

In [12]:
price_segment = pd.qcut(data["median_house_value"], 3, labels=["Low", "Medium", "High"]).astype(str)
print("Segment cut-offs ($):", data["median_house_value"].quantile([1/3, 2/3]).round(0).tolist())

X = data.drop(columns=["median_house_value"])         # inputs
y = data["median_house_value"]                        # target: the number we want to predict

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test, seg_train, seg_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, price_segment, test_size=0.2, random_state=SEED, stratify=price_segment)
print("Training neighbourhoods:", len(X_train), "| Test neighbourhoods:", len(X_test))

Segment cut-offs ($): [141400.0, 230333.0]
Training neighbourhoods: 16512 | Test neighbourhoods: 4128

3.3 The preprocessing pipeline¶

What: (1) fill missing values with the median, (2) scale numbers, (3) one-hot encode ocean_proximity. Why:

  • Median imputation: deleting rows wastes data; the median is not dragged around by giant neighbourhoods.
  • Scaling: puts every feature on a comparable scale so one measured in thousands (rooms) cannot drown out one measured in single digits (income).
  • One-hot encoding: models need numbers, so INLAND becomes a 0/1 column, and so on.

How: a ColumnTransformer applies the right steps to the right columns. Putting it inside a pipeline is crucial: the medians and scaling values are learned from the training data only, which prevents data leakage (test information sneaking into training and making our scores look better than they are).

In [13]:
num_cols = [c for c in X.columns if c != "ocean_proximity"]

preprocess = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
                      ("scale", StandardScaler())]), num_cols),
    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", sparse_output=False), ["ocean_proximity"]),
])

Xt = preprocess.fit_transform(X_train)                # fitted on TRAINING data only
print("Missing values before:", int(X_train.isna().sum().sum()), "-> after:", int(np.isnan(Xt).sum()))
print("Shape before:", X_train.shape, "-> after:", Xt.shape)
print("Final features:", [n.split("__")[1] for n in preprocess.get_feature_names_out()])

Missing values before: 340 -> after: 0
Shape before: (16512, 12) -> after: (16512, 16)
Final features: ['longitude', 'latitude', 'housing_median_age', 'total_rooms', 'total_bedrooms', 'population', 'households', 'median_income', 'rooms_per_household', 'bedrooms_per_room', 'population_per_household', 'ocean_proximity_<1H OCEAN', 'ocean_proximity_INLAND', 'ocean_proximity_ISLAND', 'ocean_proximity_NEAR BAY', 'ocean_proximity_NEAR OCEAN']

4. Build the models¶

What: set up the baseline and seven regression algorithms. Why: we want to compare different families of regression (straight lines, curves, penalised lines, trees, kernels) and see which fits this data best. The baseline (always predict the average price) is the bar every real model must clear. How: helper functions keep the code short and identical for every model:

Helper What it does
reg_pipe(model) Wraps preprocessing + a model into one pipeline
poly_preprocess(degree) Preprocessing with polynomial (curved) terms for the 4 key features
reg_metrics(...) Computes MAE, MSE, RMSE and R²
eval_reg(name, pipe) Trains a pipeline, tests it, and also reports train R² and 3-fold cross-validated R²

A lesson we learned the hard way: our first Polynomial Regression squared every feature and collapsed (R² = −20) because a few giant neighbourhoods and the five-row ISLAND category became absurd numbers once squared. We fixed it by adding curved terms only for the four main continuous drivers (POLY_COLS).

In [14]:
POLY_COLS = ["longitude", "latitude", "median_income", "housing_median_age"]   # features that get curved terms

def poly_preprocess(degree):
    base = lambda: [("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("scale", StandardScaler())]
    return ColumnTransformer([
        ("poly", Pipeline(base() + [("pf", PolynomialFeatures(degree, include_bias=False)),
                                    ("scale2", StandardScaler())]), POLY_COLS),
        ("rest", Pipeline(base()), [c for c in num_cols if c not in POLY_COLS]),
        ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", sparse_output=False), ["ocean_proximity"]),
    ])

def reg_pipe(model, degree=None):
    return Pipeline([("prep", poly_preprocess(degree) if degree else preprocess), ("model", model)])

def reg_metrics(y_true, y_pred):
    mse = mean_squared_error(y_true, y_pred)
    return dict(MAE=mean_absolute_error(y_true, y_pred), MSE=mse, RMSE=np.sqrt(mse), R2=r2_score(y_true, y_pred))

def eval_reg(name, pipe):
    pipe.fit(X_train, y_train)                                    # learn from the training data
    pred = pipe.predict(X_test)                                   # predict the hidden test data
    cv = cross_val_score(clone(pipe), X_train, y_train, cv=3, scoring="r2", n_jobs=-1).mean()
    row = dict(Model=name, **reg_metrics(y_test, pred),
               Train_R2=r2_score(y_train, pipe.predict(X_train)), CV_R2=cv)
    return row, pipe, pred

Now the models themselves. Notes on a few settings:

  • Ridge / Lasso alpha=1 is the strength of the penalty on large coefficients.
  • Random Forest builds 100 trees; random_state=SEED makes it repeatable; n_jobs=-1 uses all CPU cores.
  • SVR is wrapped in TransformedTargetRegressor so the price is also scaled; otherwise SVR underfits badly when prices are in the hundreds of thousands.
In [15]:
reg_specs = {
    "Baseline (mean)":               reg_pipe(DummyRegressor(strategy="mean")),
    "Linear Regression":             reg_pipe(LinearRegression()),
    "Polynomial Regression (deg 2)": reg_pipe(LinearRegression(), degree=2),
    "Ridge":                         reg_pipe(Ridge(alpha=1.0)),
    "Lasso":                         reg_pipe(Lasso(alpha=1.0, max_iter=10000)),
    "Decision Tree":                 reg_pipe(DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=SEED)),
    "Random Forest":                 reg_pipe(RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=100, random_state=SEED, n_jobs=-1)),
    "SVR (RBF)":                     reg_pipe(TransformedTargetRegressor(regressor=SVR(C=1.0), transformer=StandardScaler())),
}

rows, fitted, preds = [], {}, {}
for name, pipe in reg_specs.items():                  # train and evaluate every model the same way
    row, model, pred = eval_reg(name, pipe)
    rows.append(row); fitted[name] = model; preds[name] = pred
    print("done:", name)
reg_results = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("Model")

5. Evaluate the models¶

What: compare all models on the 4,128 hidden test neighbourhoods. Why: one number is not enough, so we use several complementary metrics:

Metric In plain words
MAE Average size of the mistakes, in dollars
MSE Average of the squared mistakes (punishes big errors heavily; units are dollars²)
RMSE √MSE, in dollars again; our main "typical error"
R² Share of the differences in price the model explains (1 = perfect, 0 = no better than the average)
CV R² R² averaged over 3 train/validation rotations; if it matches the test R², the result is stable
Train R² vs test R² A big gap = the model memorised the training data (overfitting)
In [16]:
fmt = {"MAE": "{:,.0f}", "MSE": "{:,.0f}", "RMSE": "{:,.0f}", "R2": "{:.3f}", "Train_R2": "{:.3f}", "CV_R2": "{:.3f}"}
display(reg_results.style.format(fmt))
print("Standard deviation of test prices (a naive model's typical error): $%.0f" % y_test.std())
  MAE MSE RMSE R2 Train_R2 CV_R2
Model            
Baseline (mean) 92,201 13,652,539,802 116,844 -0.000 0.000 -0.000
Linear Regression 49,467 4,722,036,462 68,717 0.654 0.654 0.650
Polynomial Regression (deg 2) 47,609 4,465,109,505 66,821 0.673 0.679 0.676
Ridge 49,461 4,720,196,605 68,704 0.654 0.654 0.650
Lasso 49,466 4,721,804,828 68,715 0.654 0.654 0.650
Decision Tree 44,928 4,925,558,029 70,182 0.639 1.000 0.609
Random Forest 33,025 2,544,115,622 50,439 0.814 0.974 0.804
SVR (RBF) 38,271 3,403,483,967 58,339 0.751 0.780 0.760 
Standard deviation of test prices (a naive model's typical error): $116854

How to read it

  • Every model beats the baseline (R² = 0), so the features really carry information.
  • Linear, Ridge and Lasso are practically identical (R² 0.654): with 16 features and 16,500 rows there is little overfitting for the penalties to fix, and train/test/CV scores all agree. The straight-line shape is the limit: they underfit.
  • Polynomial gives a small gain (0.673): bending the line helps a little.
  • Decision Tree is the classic overfit: train R² 1.000 but test R² only 0.639.
  • SVR generalises well (train 0.780, test 0.751).
  • Random Forest wins: R² 0.814, RMSE ≈ $50.4k. Averaging 100 trees cancels the mistakes of any single tree.

6. Look at the predictions¶

What: plot predicted price against actual price for every model, plus the train-vs-test R² gap. Why: numbers hide patterns. A good model's points hug the diagonal; the gap chart shows overfitting at a glance. How: a scatter of actual (x) vs predicted (y) with a red "perfect prediction" line.

In [17]:
names = [n for n in preds if n != "Baseline (mean)"]
lim = [y_test.min(), y_test.max()]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(17, 8))
for ax, n in zip(axes.ravel(), names):
    ax.scatter(y_test, preds[n], s=5, alpha=0.2, color=TEAL)
    ax.plot(lim, lim, "r--")                                     # perfect-prediction line
    ax.set_title(f"{n}\nR² = {reg_results.loc[n, 'R2']:.3f}", fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xlabel("actual"); ax.set_ylabel("predicted")
for ax in axes.ravel()[len(names):]: ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
In [18]:
gap = reg_results.drop(index="Baseline (mean)")[["Train_R2", "R2"]]
ax = gap.plot.bar(figsize=(10, 3.8), color=["slategray", TEAL], rot=30)
ax.set_title("Train vs test R²: a big gap means overfitting"); ax.set_ylim(0, 1.05)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

7. Hyperparameter tuning¶

What: search for better settings (hyperparameters) for each model, such as how deep a tree may grow. Why: default settings are rarely the best. But we also want to know honestly whether tuning helps. How:

  • GridSearchCV tries every combination in a small grid.
  • RandomizedSearchCV tries a limited number of random combinations (cheaper; used for the Random Forest).
  • Both use 3-fold cross-validation on the training data only, so the test set stays untouched.
  • To save time the search runs on a 6,000-row sample; the best setting is then re-trained on the full training set and tested once on the hidden data.
  • Linear Regression has no hyperparameters to tune.
In [19]:
sample_idx = X_train.sample(6000, random_state=0).index
X_s, y_s = X_train.loc[sample_idx], y_train.loc[sample_idx]

def tune_reg(name, pipe, params, kind="grid", n_iter=6):
    if kind == "grid":
        search = GridSearchCV(pipe, params, cv=3, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error", n_jobs=-1)
    else:
        search = RandomizedSearchCV(pipe, params, n_iter=n_iter, cv=3, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error",
                                    n_jobs=-1, random_state=SEED)
    search.fit(X_s, y_s)                                             # search on the sample
    best = clone(search.best_estimator_).fit(X_train, y_train)       # re-train best setting on ALL training data
    pred = best.predict(X_test)
    return dict(Model=name + " (tuned)", **reg_metrics(y_test, pred)), best, pred, search.best_params_

reg_tune = {
    "Polynomial Regression": (reg_pipe(Ridge(), degree=2), {"prep__poly__pf__degree": [1, 2, 3, 4], "model__alpha": [1, 10, 100]}, "grid"),
    "Ridge": (reg_pipe(Ridge()), {"model__alpha": [0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000]}, "grid"),
    "Lasso": (reg_pipe(Lasso(max_iter=10000)), {"model__alpha": [1, 10, 100, 1000, 5000]}, "grid"),
    "Decision Tree": (reg_pipe(DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=SEED)),
                      {"model__max_depth": [5, 8, 12, 16, None], "model__min_samples_leaf": [1, 5, 10, 20]}, "grid"),
    "Random Forest": (reg_pipe(RandomForestRegressor(random_state=SEED, n_jobs=-1)),
                      {"model__n_estimators": [100, 200], "model__max_depth": [None, 15, 25],
                       "model__min_samples_leaf": [1, 2, 5], "model__max_features": [0.33, 0.6, 1.0]}, "random"),
    "SVR (RBF)": (reg_pipe(TransformedTargetRegressor(regressor=SVR(), transformer=StandardScaler())),
                  {"model__regressor__C": [1, 10, 100], "model__regressor__gamma": ["scale", 0.05]}, "grid"),
}

tuned_rows, tuned_models, tuned_preds, summary = [], {}, {}, []
for name, (pipe, params, kind) in reg_tune.items():
    row, best, pred, best_params = tune_reg(name, pipe, params, kind)
    default_name = name if name in reg_results.index else name + " (deg 2)"
    tuned_rows.append(row); tuned_models[row["Model"]] = best; tuned_preds[row["Model"]] = pred
    summary.append({"Model": name, "Best setting": {k.split("__")[-1]: v for k, v in best_params.items()},
                    "RMSE before": round(reg_results.loc[default_name, "RMSE"]), "RMSE after": round(row["RMSE"]),
                    "R2 before": round(reg_results.loc[default_name, "R2"], 3), "R2 after": round(row["R2"], 3)})
display(pd.DataFrame(summary).set_index("Model"))

How to read it: tuning helped most where a model was clearly flawed. Pruning the Decision Tree (max_depth 16, min_samples_leaf 20) removed much of its overfitting, a higher polynomial degree gave the curve more flexibility, and SVR liked a larger C. The Ridge and Lasso penalties changed nothing (a linear model's limit is its straight-line shape, not its penalty). The tuned Random Forest was a hair *worse*** than the default (R² 0.812 vs 0.814): the difference is noise, and the search used only a sample. **So the default Random Forest stays our final model. Tuning is not magic; always check on held-out data.

8. Error analysis: where and why is the best model wrong?¶

What: study the mistakes of the Random Forest (our final model). Why: a good score is not the same as a trustworthy model. Knowing where it fails tells us how far we can trust it. How: compute the error of every test neighbourhood (actual − predicted) and slice it by price range and location.

Figure 8: predictions vs reality, and the error distribution¶

In [21]:
best_model = fitted["Random Forest"]
pred = preds["Random Forest"]
res = X_test.copy()
res["actual"], res["predicted"] = y_test, pred
res["error"] = res["actual"] - res["predicted"]                    # positive = model guessed too LOW
res["abs_pct_error"] = res["error"].abs() / res["actual"]

What to notice: about 5% of the test rows sit at the cap, yet they cause roughly 11% of all the error. Most of the biggest mistakes are expensive ($450–500k) areas priced far too low, usually places with modest income but a pricey coastal or urban location that no feature reveals. Errors are smallest inland (cheaper homes) and larger near the coast, where prices are higher and vary more.

9. Demonstration: using the saved model¶

What: save the trained Random Forest to a file, load it back, and predict prices for new locations, exactly what our web app does. Why: a model is only useful if someone can use it. This also proves our code is reproducible end to end. How:

  1. joblib.dump saves the whole pipeline (preprocessing and model) in one file, so new data is prepared automatically.
  2. predict_house_price(...) builds a one-row table, adds the same three engineered features, and calls model.predict.
  3. Like the app, we pre-fill the neighbourhood details from the 25 nearest real neighbourhoods (found with NearestNeighbors), because a user clicking a map only knows where, not the number of households.
In [25]:
joblib.dump(best_model, "random_forest_regression_model.joblib", compress=3)       # save
model = joblib.load("random_forest_regression_model.joblib")                       # load it back, as a user would
print("Saved and reloaded the final model:", type(model.named_steps["model"]).__name__)

def predict_house_price(model, longitude, latitude, housing_median_age, total_rooms, total_bedrooms,
                        population, households, median_income, ocean_proximity):
    row = pd.DataFrame([dict(longitude=longitude, latitude=latitude, housing_median_age=housing_median_age,
                             total_rooms=total_rooms, total_bedrooms=total_bedrooms, population=population,
                             households=households, median_income=median_income, ocean_proximity=ocean_proximity)])
    row["rooms_per_household"] = row["total_rooms"] / row["households"]               # same feature engineering as training
    row["bedrooms_per_room"] = row["total_bedrooms"] / row["total_rooms"]
    row["population_per_household"] = row["population"] / row["households"]
    return float(model.predict(row[X.columns])[0])

# nearest real neighbourhoods, using great-circle (haversine) distance
nn = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=25, metric="haversine").fit(np.radians(df[["latitude", "longitude"]].values))

def typical_values(lat, lon):
    _, idx = nn.kneighbors(np.radians([[lat, lon]]))
    near = df.iloc[idx[0]]
    return dict(longitude=lon, latitude=lat, housing_median_age=near["housing_median_age"].median(),
                total_rooms=near["total_rooms"].median(), total_bedrooms=near["total_bedrooms"].median(),
                population=near["population"].median(), households=near["households"].median(),
                median_income=near["median_income"].median(),
                ocean_proximity=near["ocean_proximity"].iloc[:10].mode()[0]), near["median_house_value"].mean()

Saved and reloaded the final model: RandomForestRegressor

10. Summary and lessons¶

What we did Result
Explored 20,640 neighbourhoods with 6 figures Income and location drive price; prices are capped at $500k
Engineered 3 ratio features population_per_household became the 3rd most important feature
Compared 7 algorithms + baseline Random Forest best: R² 0.814, RMSE ≈ $50.4k, MAE ≈ $33.0k (baseline RMSE ≈ $116.8k)
Tuned hyperparameters Helped the Decision Tree, Polynomial and SVR; did not help Ridge, Lasso or the Random Forest
Analysed errors Biggest errors in expensive, capped neighbourhoods; ±10% accuracy for 44% of predictions, ±20% for 70%
Built a working predictor Click a location, get a price, a likely range and a Low/Medium/High segment

Lessons we will remember

  1. Look at the data first: the price cap and the correlated size columns shaped everything after.
  2. Features and a clean pipeline matter as much as the algorithm, and leakage-proof pipelines keep scores honest.
  3. More complexity is not always better: our squared-everything polynomial failed, and tuning did not improve the winner.
  4. A good score is not the same as a trustworthy model: the error analysis shows exactly where not to trust it.

Limitations: 1990 data; prices capped at $500k; neighbourhood averages, not single houses; a random split is optimistic for brand-new regions; missing drivers such as schools and crime.

Next steps: retrain on current Indian listings (e.g. Pune) with satellite features from Google Earth Engine, use spatial cross-validation, and turn the Low/Medium/High segments into a classification model.
